html:
A French colonial agency set up in 1932 to irrigate the inland delta of the Niger in what is now Mali, then part of French West Africa. It still exists and runs one of the largest irrigated areas in West Africa.

The engineer Émile Bélime promised to water about a million hectares and grow cotton for French mills, on the model of Britain's Gezira Scheme in Sudan. The Markala Dam, finished in 1947, turned river water into the canals. The reality fell far short. Only a small part of the planned land was ever irrigated. Canals were dug by forced labour, and farmers, many of them Mossi from Upper Volta, were moved in and tightly controlled.

After independence the scheme struggled for decades. Reforms in the 1980s and 1990s gave farmers more control, and rice replaced cotton. The Office du Niger is now Mali's main source of rice. In recent years leases of its land to foreign investors have caused controversy.
sum: A French colonial agency set up in 1932 to irrigate the inland delta of the Niger in what is now Mali, then part of French West Africa. It still exists and runs one of the largest irrigated areas in West Africa.
